question: Give an example of when team dynamics were poor or conflict threatened success. What actions did you take to improve them?

raiseTranscript.text: Two devs on my feature team stopped talking after disagreeing on API design. I was blocked on my part so I scheduled a 30-min sync, wrote down both options with pros/cons, and asked each to explain their concern. We picked a middle path and finished the sprint on time.
What did you do when the first attempt didn't land?
One person still pushed back in the meeting. I asked my tech lead to join the next one and we documented the decision so everyone could reference it later.

raiseNotes: Q: Give an example of when team dynamics were poor or conflict threatened success. What actions did you take to improve them?
Role: new grad on 4-person feature team; situation: API design standoff between two mid-level devs
Actions: wrote options doc, called sync, asked tech lead to join when needed
Outcome: sprint delivered, decision documented
Quote: "I just wanted to unblock myself so I put the options on paper and got them talking."
Follow-up: Asked about escalation; candidate described looping in tech lead and writing it down
junior.raiseFeedback: The candidate described a local conflict on their feature team that was blocking their own work and took direct steps to surface options and involve the right person. They owned documenting the decision rather than waiting for someone else. This shows solid individual ownership and coachability at the junior level. The story stayed within their scope and did not claim broader team turnaround. Biggest strength is the willingness to facilitate a conversation and then escalate cleanly when needed.

lowerTranscript.text: There was tension because one person kept missing standups. I just did my work and waited for the manager to fix it.
Not really, I figured it wasn't my place as the newest person.

lowerNotes: Q: Give an example of when team dynamics were poor or conflict threatened success. What actions did you take to improve them?
Role: intern on platform team; situation: teammate missing meetings
Actions: none described beyond waiting for manager
Outcome: not stated
Quote: "I just did my work and waited for the manager to fix it."
Follow-up: Probing for personal action; candidate said it was not their place
junior.lowerFeedback: The candidate identified a dynamic issue but took no visible action and explicitly deferred to the manager without attempting even a low-risk step. At junior level we expect some ownership of their immediate environment and willingness to try simple interventions. The response shows passivity rather than the coachability and initiative we look for. Biggest gap is absence of any attempt to improve the situation themselves before escalating.

raiseTranscript.text: Two backend teams had overlapping ownership on a shared service and were rejecting each other's PRs. I set up a joint design review, mapped the disputed areas on a whiteboard, and proposed a narrow interface contract both leads signed off on.
How did you get the second team to engage?
I went to their manager first with data on how many reviews were bouncing, then invited their senior engineer to co-own the contract definition.

raiseNotes: Q: Give an example of when team dynamics were poor or conflict threatened success. What actions did you take to improve them?
Role: senior engineer; situation: two backend teams rejecting PRs on shared service
Actions: initiated joint design review, created narrow interface contract, enlisted second team's manager and senior engineer
Outcome: contract signed, review velocity improved
Quote: "I brought the data on rejected PRs to their manager so they saw it wasn't just noise."
Follow-up: How engagement was secured; candidate described pre-work with the other manager
senior.raiseFeedback: The candidate used influence across team boundaries by bringing data to the other manager and creating a joint artifact both sides could own. They stayed within senior scope by focusing on a concrete interface rather than attempting to reorganize teams. The approach shows cross-team collaboration without authority. Biggest strength is the step of pre-aligning with the second manager before the broader meeting.

lowerTranscript.text: I tried to mediate between the two teams but they kept arguing in the meeting so I stopped scheduling them.
What happened to the underlying ownership issue?
It stayed the same. Eventually leadership re-orged the teams.

lowerNotes: Q: Give an example of when team dynamics were poor or conflict threatened success. What actions did you take to improve them?
Role: senior; situation: inter-team PR rejections
Actions: scheduled meetings that devolved into arguments
Outcome: gave up and waited for re-org
Quote: "I tried to mediate but they kept arguing so I stopped scheduling them."
Follow-up: Probing persistence; candidate described stopping without alternative path
senior.lowerFeedback: The candidate attempted facilitation but abandoned the effort when the first meetings failed and relied on an eventual re-org they did not influence. At senior level we expect persistence and alternative approaches such as smaller bilateral conversations or data-driven framing. The story shows limited cross-team influence and quick retreat. Biggest gap is lack of follow-through after initial resistance.

raiseTranscript.text: Two of my teams had a long-running feud over API changes that was slowing a critical launch. I held separate 1:1s with the leads to understand the root concerns, then ran a working session where each team presented their constraints and we agreed on a phased rollout plan with clear owners.
How did you handle the lead who was most resistant?
I asked him to own the communication plan to the broader org so he had skin in the outcome and his concerns were visible.

raiseNotes: Q: Give an example of when team dynamics were poor or conflict threatened success. What actions did you take to improve them?
Role: engineering manager of two teams; situation: API change feud threatening launch
Actions: separate 1:1s, joint working session, gave resistant lead ownership of communication plan
Outcome: phased plan agreed, launch unblocked
Quote: "I gave the most resistant lead ownership of the comms plan so his concerns became part of the solution."
Follow-up: Handling resistance; candidate described converting resistor into owner
manager.raiseFeedback: The candidate addressed team dynamics by first diagnosing root concerns individually then creating a structured forum with clear ownership. They used a classic manager lever by giving the resistant lead a visible role that aligned incentives. The story demonstrates handling underperformance in collaboration and creating leverage through the team. Biggest strength is the deliberate step of converting resistance into ownership rather than forcing consensus.

lowerTranscript.text: I told both teams to work it out and escalated to my director when nothing changed.
What did you do before escalating?
I sent a couple of emails reminding them of the launch date.

lowerNotes: Q: Give an example of when team dynamics were poor or conflict threatened success. What actions did you take to improve them?
Role: manager; situation: inter-team feud on API changes
Actions: sent reminder emails then escalated
Outcome: relied on director
Quote: "I told both teams to work it out and escalated when nothing changed."
Follow-up: Probing manager actions; candidate described only email reminders
manager.lowerFeedback: The candidate treated the conflict as something the teams should resolve themselves and moved quickly to escalation without structured intervention. At manager level we expect active coaching of leads and creation of forums that surface constraints. The approach shows limited investment in developing the team's collaboration skills. Biggest gap is absence of 1:1 diagnosis or ownership transfer before escalation.

raiseTranscript.text: Two product orgs were duplicating work and blaming each other for missed revenue targets. I created a joint OKR around shared platform reuse, moved one senior leader into a dotted-line role across both groups, and tracked the reduction in duplicate headcount requests in quarterly reviews.
We delayed one org's feature by a quarter so the shared component could be built once; I communicated the bet to the CEO and absorbed the short-term metric hit.

raiseNotes: Q: Give an example of when team dynamics were poor or conflict threatened success. What actions did you take to improve them?
Role: VP; situation: two product orgs duplicating work and finger-pointing
Actions: joint OKR, dotted-line leadership role, tracked duplicate headcount in reviews
Outcome: reduced duplication, one quarter delay accepted
Quote: "I moved one leader into a dotted-line role across both groups so the conflict had a single owner."
Follow-up: Trade-offs accepted; candidate described absorbing short-term metric impact with CEO
exec.raiseFeedback: The candidate operated at org scale by changing incentives and reporting lines rather than mediating individual disputes. They accepted a visible short-term cost and owned the narrative upward. This reflects strategic judgment on when to restructure collaboration mechanisms. Biggest strength is the willingness to take a metric hit in exchange for long-term leverage across organizations.

lowerTranscript.text: I asked the two VPs to meet weekly until they sorted out the overlap.
They continued to escalate decisions to me so I eventually made the call on which features to cut.

lowerNotes: Q: Give an example of when team dynamics were poor or conflict threatened success. What actions did you take to improve them?
Role: exec; situation: overlapping product work between two orgs
Actions: told VPs to meet weekly
Outcome: decisions kept escalating upward
Quote: "I asked the two VPs to meet weekly until they sorted it out."
Follow-up: Probing structural change; candidate described continuing to arbitrate
exec.lowerFeedback: The candidate relied on a recurring meeting between peers without altering incentives or decision rights. At exec level we look for changes to org structure, goals, or accountability that prevent repeated escalation. The story shows continued personal arbitration rather than systemic resolution. Biggest gap is absence of structural levers or acceptance of short-term trade-offs.
